U1A.title: A MYSTERIOUS VISITOR
U1A.content: A In October 2017, astronomers in Hawaii saw something surprising. A strange object was moving through the solar system. They had seen many asteroids before, but this was something different. It was long and thin—like a cucumber. The object's speed and direction also showed something surprising. This was an interstellar object—the first ever seen. B The object was named 'Oumuamua—Hawaiian for 'visitor from afar.' Nobody is sure exactly what it is. The simplest idea is that 'Oumuamua is a strangely shaped piece of rock. Perhaps it was knocked out of a far-off star system. However, astronomers saw that its speed increased after passing the sun. Some scientists therefore suggest a different theory. C 'Oumuamua could be a piece of alien technology, says Professor Abraham Loeb from Harvard University. Loeb believes this could explain the object's long, thin shape, and also its change in speed. Maybe 'Oumuamua was a spaceship that came to explore our solar system. All possibilities should be considered, says Loeb. D 'Oumuamua can no longer be seen from Earth. But astronomers continue to study the information they got from it. It is still not clear if the object was a large rock, or something else altogether. 'Oumuamua will likely be a mystery for many years to come.

U1B.title: THE LOST CITY OF ATLANTIS
U1B.content: A Most people have heard the story of the lost city of Atlantis. But is any part of the story true? Over two thousand years ago, the Greek writer Plato wrote about Atlantis, an island in the Atlantic Ocean. The island's people were very rich. They built a big city with many great buildings. But the people became greedy—they had many things, but they still wanted more. So the gods became angry. B Earthquakes and large waves began to strike the island. Finally, Atlantis sank into the sea. For years, people have looked for the lost city. Some think it was near Greece. Others believe it was near Spain, or even in the Atlantic Ocean. C However, many archeologists think Atlantis never really existed. They believe Plato invented the story to teach a lesson. He wanted to warn people about what can happen when they become too rich and greedy. D Today, the story of Atlantis is still popular in books and movies. The mystery of the lost city continues to fascinate people all over the world.

U2A.title: THE WORLD OF SPEED EATING
U2A.content: A Competitive eating—or speed eating—is exactly what its name suggests. Contestants eat as much as they can, usually within a time limit. Eating competitions can involve various foods—pizza, pies, ice cream, chili peppers. They can also offer large prizes to the winners. B Many of the world's top competitive eaters come from Japan and the United States. One famous eater is Takeru Kobayashi. He became famous when he ate 50 hot dogs in 12 minutes at a competition in New York. Another top competitor is Joey Chestnut, who later broke Kobayashi's record by eating 74 hot dogs in 10 minutes. C How do these people eat so much so quickly? Many stretch their stomachs by drinking large amounts of water before a contest. They also exercise to stay fit, as a fit body helps them digest food faster. D However, doctors warn that speed eating can be dangerous. Eating too much food too quickly can cause serious health problems. Despite the risks, competitive eating remains a popular and growing sport.

U2B.title: THE BIG MATCH
U2B.content: A Major competitive teams prepare for months before a match. Every single participant trains intensely. B Workers often competed to see whose team could do a job faster. In ancient building sites, teams left colorful marks on stones. C These marks showed which group carved or moved the block. Friendly competition kept the massive projects moving on schedule.

U3A.title: BRAIN SOUNDS
U3A.content: A Sound waves travel through the air and hit our eardrums. The brain instantly translates these vibrations into recognizable music or voices. B Neuroscientists study how different sound patterns create specific emotional responses. Upbeat rhythms can instantly release dopamine, making people feel happy.

U3B.title: THE POWER OF MUSIC
U3B.content: A Music seems to activate different parts of the brain, including the damaged parts. For example, it can help people who have trouble speaking or remembering things after an illness. Musicians often have larger brains than other people. B Music also has the power to change our mood. Fast music can make us feel energetic, while slow music can help us relax. Some doctors use music therapy to help patients deal with pain and stress. C In addition, music can improve our memory. Many people find it easier to remember information when it is set to a song. This is why children often learn the alphabet through singing. D In short, music is a powerful tool that affects both our brain and our body in amazing ways.

U4A.title: DEEP SEA MYSTERIES
U4A.content: A The deep ocean remains largely unexplored. Massive pressures and absolute darkness make it hard for regular submersibles to navigate safely. B Autonomous underwater vehicles carry advanced sonar grids to map the vast ocean floor, discovering bizarre life forms near thermal vents.

U4B.title: MY DESCENT TO THE TITANIC
U4B.content: A In 2001, I was part of an expedition to explore the Titanic. The famous ship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg, and now lies deep on the ocean floor. B Our team used two small deep-sea robots, one blue and one green. My job was to make sure the robots' batteries worked well. Three days into the expedition, the green robot got stuck inside the Titanic. Even worse, one of its batteries was damaged. That was dangerous, as the battery could explode. It could harm the robot and the ship. We had to find a way to get it out. C Fortunately, the team managed to rescue the green robot using the blue one. It was a difficult operation that took several hours, but both robots returned safely to the surface. D The expedition was a success, and we collected valuable images and data that will help scientists understand how the ship is changing over time.

U5A.title: MONEY HISTORY
U5A.content: A Before paper bills existed, ancient people traded goods directly. Later, communities used rare seashells, salt, or heavy metal coins to represent standardized value. B Precious metals like gold and silver became the global standard because they were durable and hard to find.

U5B.title: DIGITAL CASH
U5B.content: A Modern transactions happen in milliseconds through digital wires. Virtual currency and mobile applications are slowly reshaping how global economies operate daily. B Physical wallets are being replaced by biometric encryptions, making global banking faster but introducing new cyber security risks.

U6A.title: ANIMAL IQ
U6A.content: A Many animals possess advanced problem-solving skills that surprise researchers. Crows can construct complex tools from wire, and octopuses can escape intricate glass mazes easily. B Dolphins display self-awareness by recognizing their reflections in mirrors, a trait shared with only a few highly intelligent species.

U6B.title: THE VENUS FLYTRAP
U6B.content: A The Venus flytrap is a unique predatory plant native to subtropical wetlands. It waits silently for insects to touch its tiny sensory hairs before snapping shut instantly. B Once triggered, the leaf secretes strong digestive fluids to dissolve the insect, absorbing crucial nutrients that are missing from the poor soil.

U7A.title: VISUAL TRICKS
U7A.content: A Our eyes capture light, but our mind interprets the final meaning. This functional gap allows specific geometric patterns to warp our visual perception. B Optical artists manipulate lines, colors, and shadows to create static images that appear to rotate or pulse dynamically before our eyes.

U7B.title: SEEING THE IMPOSSIBLE
U7B.content: A Can you believe everything you see? Not always! Sometimes our minds and our eyes make mistakes and get confused. This may be because we are looking at an optical illusion. B The word optical means 'related to sight'—the way we see things. An illusion is something that looks different from the way it really is. In short, an optical illusion is a trick that our eyes play on us. C Look at these optical illusions and compare what you see with what your classmates see. At a first look, most people say 'No.' D But if you compare the lines against an object with a straight edge, you'll see otherwise. The small circles in the squares help create the illusion. Our brain tries to make sense of the patterns, but ends up misinterpreting the actual straight lines.

U8A.title: ANCIENT MYTHS
U8A.content: A Every ancient culture built detailed legends around stars. Constellations served as seasonal farming maps and religious blueprints across generations. B Navigators used the North Star as an absolute anchor, guiding wooden ships safely across featureless oceans before compasses were engineered.

U8B.title: THE GREEK WRITERS
U8B.content: A Early Greek literature provided the structural pillars for Western storytelling, diving deep into human flaws, pride, and tragic destiny. B Playwrights used dramatic irony to engage audiences, creating complex theatrical scripts that are still performed in modern theaters worldwide.

U9A.title: WEATHER FORCE
U9A.content: A Superstorms hold immense atmospheric energy. Rapidly rising warm air currents generate massive friction, producing violent electrical lightning strikes. B Tracking lightning pathways with satellite arrays helps meteorologists warn cities early, protecting high-risk electrical power grids from severe damage.

U9B.title: SMOKE JUMPERS
U9B.content: A Wildfire response teams jump directly from airplanes into active remote forests. They carry heavy axes and shovels to clear out dry vegetation. B By removing burnable materials like dry grass and dead trees, smoke jumpers create an absolute barrier to starve advancing flame lines successfully.

U10A.title: EGYPTIAN LIFE
U10A.content: A Life along the ancient Nile was highly structured and communal. Entire farming communities relied heavily on the river's predictable annual floods to irrigate fields. B Beyond agriculture, citizens contributed seasonal labor to build state monuments, receiving food and clothes as compensation from the royal courts.

U10B.title: TOMBS OF KINGS
U10B.content: A Royal burial chambers were hidden deep inside massive stone structures. Architects designed complex corridors to protect the pharaoh's treasures from thieves. B Artists covered internal walls with vivid hieroglyphics, telling stories of military victories and documenting the king's journey into the afterlife.

U11A.title: TURTLE RESCUE
U11A.content: A Conservationists track endangered sea turtles across massive oceanic pathways. Marine teams work around the clock to remove plastic hazards lodged deep inside their airways. B Publicizing these rescue videos online raises global awareness, forcing companies to reconsider plastic packaging laws to protect ocean life.

U11B.title: ANIMAL TRACKING
U11B.content: A Advanced satellite tags allow marine biologists to study long-range migratory patterns in real time without disrupting natural wildlife habits. B Gathering coordinates on whale movements helps global shipping companies adjust transit lanes, preventing fatal vessel collisions with migrating pods.

U12A.title: ROBOT FUTURE
U12A.content: A Automation handles highly repetitive industrial operations easily. Mechanical arms weld automobile chassis with absolute precision and zero fatigue. B As AI systems assume routine data management, human operators can focus entirely on creative design and strategic problem solving.

U12B.title: THE YEAR 2045
U12B.content: A Imagine waking up in the year 2045. Your home knows exactly when you wake up and prepares your favorite breakfast automatically. B Science has found amazing ways to keep people healthy. Nanotechnology can help cure many illnesses, including cancer. You might live to be 120 years old. C As you get dressed, you say to your shirt, 'Turn red.' It becomes red instantly. In 2045, smart clothing contains nanoparticles that carry electricity. So you can program clothes to change colors or patterns based on your mood.

U1A.title: THE INCREDIBLE DOLPHIN
U1A.content: A Many people say dolphins are intelligent. They seem to be able to think, understand, and learn things quickly. But are they as smart as humans, or are they more like cats and dogs? Dolphins use their brains quite differently from the way people do. But scientists say dolphins and humans are alike in some ways. How? B Communication: Like humans, every dolphin has its own 'name.' The name is a special whistle. Each dolphin chooses a whistle for itself, usually by its first birthday. Dolphins are like people in other ways, too. They 'talk' to each other about a lot of things—such as their age, their feelings, and possible danger. They also use a system of sounds and body language to communicate. Understanding dolphin conversation is not easy for humans. No one 'speaks dolphin' yet, but some scientists are trying to learn. C Play: Dolphins live in groups called pods, and they often join other dolphins from different pods to play games and have fun—just like people. Sometimes they chase other dolphins carrying objects (e.g., seaweed) and throw these objects back and forth. Scientists believe playing together is something only intelligent animals do. D Teamwork: Dolphins and humans are similar in another way: They both make plans for getting things they want. In the seas of southern Brazil, for example, dolphins use an intelligent method to get food. When there are fish near a boat, dolphins signal to the fishermen to put the nets down. Then the dolphins drive the fish toward the nets. The fishermen catch the fish, and the dolphins get some too. This intelligent teamwork benefits both humans and dolphins.

U1B.title: DOLPHIN TEAMWORK
U1B.content: A In the coastal waters of southern Brazil, a unique partnership has formed between local fishermen and wild bottlenose dolphins. This cooperative hunting has been happening for over a century. B When a school of mullet fish approaches the shore, the dolphins dive under the water, driving the fish toward the shallow coastal line where the men stand with their casting nets. C The water is muddy, so the fishermen cannot see the fish at all. They must wait for a specific signal from the dolphins—a sudden, forceful head slap or a distinct splash on the water surface. D The moment the dolphin signals, the men throw their nets. The nets capture large numbers of fish, while the panicked fish that escape run straight into the waiting jaws of the dolphins. Neither side could catch this many fish without the other's intelligent cooperation.

U2A.title: CHIMPANZEE BEHAVIOR
U2A.content: A Primates display highly complex social structures and deep emotional bonds. In the dense jungles of Gombe, young chimpanzees observe tribal elders closely for years to inherit essential foraging techniques. B They learn how to select flexible twigs, strip off the leaves carefully, and insert them into termite mounds to fish for rich protein sources. C Furthermore, chimpanzees communicate using over thirty distinct vocalizations and gestures. They express comfort through mutual grooming sessions, which reduce tension within the pod community and reinforce political alliances among alpha males.

U2B.title: MONKEY TOOLS
U2B.content: A Capuchin monkeys in Brazil demonstrate an extraordinary understanding of simple tool usage. When foraging for food, they select heavy, flat stones to serve as natural anvils. B They then search for hard palm nuts, placing them carefully on the stone platform before striking them forcefully with another large rock hammer. C This complex action requires significant planning, force calibration, and years of practice. Young capuchins watch their parents intently, picking up discarded hammers to practice on softer husks before attempting to crack hard nuts independently.

U3A.title: CITIZEN SCIENTISTS
U3A.content: A How can a regular person become a citizen scientist? It's easy. First, find a project that you like online. One of my favorites is iNaturalist, which studies diverse animals and plants globally. B Then, download the project's application and use your smartphone to take clear pictures. For example, you can photograph different kinds of rare trees or insects near your home or school. C When you're done, upload your photos to iNaturalist. If you don't know the exact name of an animal or plant, other community experts can tell you. It's a great way to learn about your environment, and you also assist professional scientists with their active research datasets directly.

U3B.title: THE LOST LADYBUG PROJECT
U3B.content: A For many years, entomologists in North America thought the native nine-spotted ladybug was completely extinct due to invasive species. B Then citizen scientist Peter Priolo photographed the rare insect in New York while participating in a casual nature walk. He sent his photo to the Lost Ladybug Project, a site that is creating a detailed map of different ladybug species distributions. C Thanks to thousands of uploaded photos from citizen scientists across the country, professional researchers now know something important: The nine-spotted ladybug is exceptionally rare, but definitely not extinct. This crowdsourced data allows maps to be updated in real time.

U4A.title: SHARK TRACKERS
U4A.content: A Marine biologists attach sophisticated satellite tracking tags to great white sharks to map the apex predators' vast oceanic movements. B Understanding where sharks hunt and mate allows international agencies to establish protected marine sanctuaries, keeping fragile coastal ecosystems balanced and safe from overfishing.

U4B.title: REEF PROTECTION
U4B.content: A Coral reefs are the rainforests of the sea, supporting thousands of marine species. However, rising temperatures and pollution are causing massive bleaching events. B Local communities are constructing innovative artificial concrete structures underwater. These shapes encourage rapid coral regrowth and successfully restore depleted fish populations back to historical levels.

U5A.title: VOLCANO ADVENTURE
U5A.content: A Geologists risk their lives descending directly into active volcanic vents to collect fresh gas samples and measure thermal fluctuations. B Analyzing these chemical combinations allows research teams to predict upcoming eruption patterns accurately, providing crucial evacuation windows that save thousands of lives.

U5B.title: EARTHQUAKE ZONE
U5B.content: A Tectonic plate shifts release massive amounts of energy, generating destructive shockwaves through urban centers. B Modern seismic engineering allows skyscrapers to sway safely during quakes. Using large base isolators and dampers, these advanced systems keep structural integrity intact, protecting residents effectively.

U6A.title: MARS ROVER EXPLORATION
U6A.content: A Robotic rovers navigate the freezing, rough Martian valleys autonomously. They carry advanced drill assemblies to collect deep core soil samples. B These samples are analyzed inside onboard chemical laboratories to detect organic molecules or chemical signatures of ancient bacterial life that may have thrived billions of years ago.

U6B.title: SPACE STATION LIFE
U6B.content: A Living in zero gravity requires astronauts to maintain strict daily schedules. Without gravity, human muscles and bones deteriorate rapidly over time. B Crew members spend two hours every day on specialized resistance exercise machines, serving as crucial test subjects for long-duration human spaceflight biology.

U7A.title: THE TRUTH ABOUT DINOSAURS
U7A.content: A Dinosaurs are fascinating, but half-truths and myths about them are common. For years, scientists thought dinosaurs were just giant, slow-moving reptiles. Some dinosaurs were indeed huge. But many were actually about the size of modern-day birds or dogs. B Were dinosaurs warm-or cold-blooded? Paleontologists are still not entirely sure. But they now believe a few dinosaurs were quite intelligent. Some smaller ones—like the two-meter Troodon—had fairly large brains relative to their bodies, suggesting advanced hunting behaviors.

U7B.title: PREDATOR OR SCAVENGER
U7B.content: A While some scientists think Tyrannosaurus rex was a powerful, fast predator, others think the opposite is true. In reality, though, this dinosaur could not run very fast. B It was simply too large to move quickly, so it probably moved about as fast as an elephant. T.rex also had very small arms and probably wasn't a powerful hunter. It may have been a scavenger instead, using its massive sense of smell to find dead animals.

U8A.title: GLACIER TREK
U8A.content: A Alpine research teams trek across massive moving ice sheets to log climate transformations accurately. They measure ice core density and track melting rates. B Documenting these rapid changes helps scientists project global sea-level rises and secure fresh drinking water routes for populations living down the mountain valleys.

U8B.title: DEEP CAVE EXPLORATION
U8B.content: A Speleologists navigate vertical underground tunnels, descending thousands of meters into absolute darkness where human feet have never stepped. B They catalog unique subterranean species that survive completely without sunlight, unlocking biological mysteries about how life adapts to extreme, high-pressure environments.

U9A.title: ANCIENT NAVIGATION
U9A.content: A Early Polynesian voyagers crossed massive stretches of the Pacific Ocean using only natural signs. They read wave behaviors, tracked bird migrations, and memorized stellar pathways perfectly. B Without any magnetic compasses or instruments, these master navigators successfully settled distant island chains across thousands of miles.

U9B.title: THE FIRST MAPS
U9B.content: A Early geographic charts combined factual coastlines with highly imaginative myths. Cartographers drew elaborate sea monsters in unexplored waters to indicate danger. B These historic maps showcase both a desire for territorial discovery and a profound psychological fear of the unknown world beyond the horizon.

U10A.title: THE PYRAMIDS ARCHITECTURE
U10A.content: A Modern engineers admire the extreme precision of early Egyptian monument alignments. Massive limestone blocks weighing several tons were moved across desert sands. B These blocks were perfectly squared and positioned to follow cardinal directions precisely, showcasing a deep understanding of structural geometry and astronomy.

U10B.title: THE PYRAMID BUILDERS
U10B.content: A It took about 80 years to build the pyramids. Archeologists believe that about 20,000–30,000 people were involved in the construction. The workers had different roles. Some dug up the rock, some moved it, and some shaped it into blocks. B People also worked on different teams, each with its own name. Workers often competed to see whose team could do a job faster. Close by, there is a cemetery where the pyramid builders were buried. From studying the bodies, archeologists know that the work was difficult.

U11A.title: GREAT INVENTIONS
U11A.content: A Simple mechanical gears transformed human manufacturing speeds during the Industrial Revolution. Automated looms turned raw cotton into fabric at incredible speeds. B This shift allowed small craft operations to scale into massive global industries, changing consumer economies and urban landscapes forever.

U11B.title: PRINTING PRESS IMPACT
U11B.content: A Movable type allowed scientific thoughts and political ideas to spread rapidly across continents. Books became affordable to the general public for the first time. B This democratization of information sparked massive literacy campaigns and built modern educational systems within a few generations.

U12A.title: LOST IN FLIGHT
U12A.content: A Early aviation pioneers challenged distance records continuously, flying wooden aircraft across oceans. Without modern radar, navigation relied heavily on precise star sights. B Pilots faced volatile weather patterns and unpredictable radio failures, risking their lives to map out the early commercial flight paths we use today.

U12B.title: AMELIA EARHART MYSTERY
U12B.content: A What happened to Amelia Earhart? No one knows for sure. In 1937, she was attempting to fly around the world when her plane disappeared over the Pacific Ocean. B During the flight, she likely headed in the wrong direction because the sun was bright and it was hard to see. Perhaps she and Noonan got lost somewhere over the open water; soon after, her plane ran out of gas, and she crashed into the sea. Today, people are still actively investigating Earhart's and Noonan's disappearance.
